nodes.label: scorsese (cross-platform video editor for agentic workflows)
nodes.rationale: Built so a human or a Claude agent assembles a video from a JSON project file and renders it headlessly; the GUI exists only for humans to scrub, tweak and review.
nodes.norm_label: scorsese (cross-platform video editor for agentic workflows)

nodes.label: North star — realize the envisioned video fastest
nodes.rationale: Claude must be able to carry the whole editing process from prompts plus user-provided files; the GUI is only a visualization of the editing plan. Any add/edit to the codebase MUST add to this vision.
nodes.norm_label: north star — realize the envisioned video fastest

nodes.label: Scope rule — approachable editor, not a compositing suite
nodes.rationale: Cuts, titles, music, narration, pacing are in scope; node graphs, tracking, rotoscoping, colour pipelines and VFX are a different craft and a different program. A capability that only makes sense to a professional editor is probably out; the rule cuts both ways — it justifies refusing an elaborate feature and equally justifies building an obvious one well.
nodes.norm_label: scope rule — approachable editor, not a compositing suite

nodes.label: Filmora 9 as reference for taste
nodes.rationale: Reference for 'what should this feel like?', never a specification. Copy in spirit: built-in animations and fonts, audio volume as plain linear ramps between points, speed changes on video and audio. Ignore anything that exists because a professional demanded it.

nodes.label: A project is a directory (*.scor/)
nodes.rationale: project.json + assets/ (copied on import) + generated/ (content-addressed by brief hash) + recipes/ (authored, not rebuildable) + cache/ (rebuildable, gitignored). All paths relative to the project root and no absolute paths ever, so a project survives `scp -r` between machines.

nodes.label: project.json — the format contract
nodes.rationale: The contract between the CLI, the MCP server, the GUI and every saved project — so format changes are `architecture`-label work and require a schema version bump plus a migration note.

nodes.label: Assets are entities, clips are references
nodes.rationale: Assets table holds id, kind, path, sha256 and probed metadata; tracks hold clips that reference assets by id, never by path, so two clips can share one asset. Kinds: video, image, audio, text, generated_video (Veo), generated_audio (ElevenLabs TTS), synth_audio (synthesis recipe).
nodes.norm_label: assets are entities, clips are references

nodes.label: Generated-asset sketch lifecycle (sketch → queued → generated → stale)
nodes.rationale: Sketch/stale clips render as slug cards so a full preview cut costs $0; GO realises only sketch/stale assets and output is cached by the hash of its brief, so an unchanged brief is never paid for twice. Stale = brief edited after generation.
nodes.norm_label: generated-asset sketch lifecycle (sketch → queued → generated → stale)

nodes.label: Prompt brief (paid, networked, irreproducible)
nodes.rationale: A sentence handed to a provider: costs money, needs a network, cannot be reproduced from the project alone.

nodes.label: Recipe brief (free, offline, deterministic)
nodes.rationale: A document in recipes/ that synthesis reads locally, for free, deterministically. An asset carries exactly the brief its kind takes and never the other — the distinction is load-bearing and must not be collapsed.

nodes.label: AssetKind::is_prompted / is_synthesized / is_generated
nodes.rationale: The code-level encoding of the prompt-vs-recipe split: two predicates under a shared is_generated, deliberately not collapsed back together.

nodes.label: Path B — compositing is ours, ffmpeg only decodes and encodes
nodes.rationale: ffmpeg decodes sources to raw frames, our compositor produces each output frame (transforms, alpha, text), raw frames are piped to ffmpeg stdin for encode. Render settings (aspect, resolution, fps, bitrate) are user-chosen per render, never stored.
nodes.norm_label: path b — compositing is ours, ffmpeg only decodes and encodes

nodes.label: Generic keyframes — (property_path, [(t, value, easing)])
nodes.rationale: A keyframe track animates any numeric property; position, scale and opacity come first but the mechanism must not know which property it animates.

nodes.label: Generality rule — core defines property types, never property values
nodes.rationale: We make text colour choosable; we never write 'make text red'. Keeps the core a mechanism rather than a catalogue of specific effects.
nodes.norm_label: generality rule — core defines property types, never property values

nodes.label: Audio is first-class
nodes.rationale: Audio tracks with keyframable volume; auto-ducking of music under narration is a planned feature, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: core and cli never touch a display
nodes.rationale: No window, no GPU surface, no GUI toolkit — stated in each lib.rs doc and enforced in review, so the GUI is a client of the same library logic the CLI and MCP server use rather than a privileged path.
nodes.norm_label: core and cli never touch a display

nodes.label: The GUI is egui, in Rust, deliberately thin
nodes.rationale: One language and one toolchain, and a compositor frame reaches the screen as a texture rather than crossing a process boundary — that is what makes scrubbing feel immediate. It gets only what a person reaches for with a mouse, often (scrub, select, nudge, trim, plain values); anything with structure is a sentence to an assistant over MCP, because a GUI rich enough to do the editing would be a second, weaker way to do everything.
nodes.norm_label: the gui is egui, in rust, deliberately thin

nodes.label: Ship it simple, then iterate from use
nodes.rationale: The GUI's requirements cannot be reasoned out in advance, so the bar for a first version is 'the user can start editing with it', not 'it is right'. Perfecting an untried interaction is the failure mode to avoid.
nodes.norm_label: ship it simple, then iterate from use

nodes.label: MCP is a protocol, not a Claude feature
nodes.rationale: crates/mcp speaks MCP to whatever client is on the other end — Gemini, GPT, anything — the way an HTTP API does not care whether a browser, a phone or curl is calling. Claude is who we develop and test against, not a dependency; nothing in the server may assume otherwise.
nodes.norm_label: mcp is a protocol, not a claude feature

nodes.label: crates/compositor — frame rendering, CPU tiny-skia first
nodes.rationale: CPU tiny-skia first is settled architecture, not a consequence of the dev machine's GPU; wgpu comes later behind the same trait.
nodes.norm_label: crates/compositor — frame rendering, cpu tiny-skia first

nodes.label: crates/zimmer — synthesis, recipe documents to samples
nodes.rationale: No I/O at all and no dependency on core, so synthesis stays a pure document-to-samples function.
nodes.norm_label: crates/zimmer — synthesis, recipe documents to samples

nodes.label: crates/providers — Veo + ElevenLabs + synthesis, brief-hash cache
nodes.norm_label: crates/providers — veo + elevenlabs + synthesis, brief-hash cache

nodes.label: crates/mcp — MCP server, thin wrapper over the same logic
nodes.norm_label: crates/mcp — mcp server, thin wrapper over the same logic

nodes.label: crates/golden — the golden-render gate harness
nodes.rationale: Test infrastructure that nothing ships and nothing depends on.

nodes.label: The zimmer naming rule (rename stops at the crate boundary)
nodes.rationale: The project is named for Martin Scorsese, the synthesis crate for Hans Zimmer — surname only, both times. Not a vendor, not a dependency, not an acronym. The name says nothing about what the crate does, so its lib.rs first line ('sound from a document') must, and missing_docs is a merge gate so that line cannot go missing. `scorsese synth`, the synth_* MCP tools and "kind": "synth_audio" all stay, because an agent-facing surface has to describe itself and the asset kind is the format contract.
nodes.norm_label: the zimmer naming rule (rename stops at the crate boundary)

nodes.label: One machine, one person (Ryzen 5 3400G, 16 GB, RTX 2060, Arch)
nodes.rationale: Written down so nobody re-derives the industry default of many contributors on many cold machines. 8 threads and 16 GB mean worktrees are cheap but simultaneous builds are not (rustc linking runs out of memory), a warm target/ is the fast path so sccache is the wrong trade, and anything GPU-dependent can be tried here but can never be a merge gate.
nodes.norm_label: one machine, one person (ryzen 5 3400g, 16 gb, rtx 2060, arch)

nodes.label: CI is a different computer
nodes.rationale: GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04: cold, no GPU, and often a different ffmpeg build than the rolling-release Arch box that produced a frame locally. 'Works here' and 'passes CI' are separate claims — which is why golden renders compare frames with tolerance rather than encoded bytes.

nodes.label: The three gates — Understanding, Value, Craft
nodes.rationale: An idea becomes an issue only when all three hold; if any fails, push back instead of complying. Agent velocity is part of Craft, not a trade-off against it.
nodes.norm_label: the three gates — understanding, value, craft

nodes.label: Draft vs ready pull requests
nodes.rationale: A ready PR claims it passes; a draft makes no such claim, and CI runs only on ready PRs and main. Draft is how work survives the three cases where pushing is the point (a question for the user, CI red after the ~3-attempts rule, a run stopped mid-work) — none asserts completion, so a red run always means a broken claim and deserves a notification. A red ready PR stays ready and is fixed in the next commit. Nothing depends on a hand-back comment existing; the durable context is the issue, written to be read cold.

nodes.label: make gates — every gate CI blocks on
nodes.rationale: Run before marking a PR ready, deliberately not before every push: GitHub should not be the first thing that compiles the code, and checkpoint commits must stay cheap. `make help` lists the targets, so the target list — not ci.yml — answers 'what has to be green?'. The app gate is the only conditional one and reports as skipped rather than green over a check that did not run.
nodes.norm_label: make gates — every gate ci blocks on

nodes.label: make mergeable PR=N
nodes.rationale: Not optional and its answer is not negotiable: it asks GitHub whether a run genuinely happened on the head commit, because 'the checks look green' and 'the checks ran' are different claims. Issue #153 is what happens when they diverge — a ready PR whose only run was a skipped one reads as passing and compiled nothing. `gh pr checks` blends runs and is not a substitute.

nodes.label: One worktree per issue, every unblocked issue at once
nodes.rationale: Isolation is what makes a branch's gates mean anything — a shared checkout mixes another issue's edits into make gates and thrashes target/. Re-read the board after every merge, not after a batch: priority orders what gets merged, never what gets worked, and an unblocked issue left unstarted is capacity going to waste.
nodes.norm_label: one worktree per issue, every unblocked issue at once

nodes.label: Serialized merging, one PR at a time
nodes.rationale: Rust is compiled: two PRs can each be green alone yet break main together, so merging cannot be parallelized. Merge queues and speculative CI answer a question this repo does not have — at one contributor, rebase-and-verify is a minute by hand. Markdown-only PRs are the one exception, and docs/project-format.md is not one of them because tests parse it.
nodes.norm_label: serialized merging, one pr at a time

nodes.label: Size gate — 300 LOC source, 150 LOC test
nodes.rationale: Blank and comment lines do not count, because missing_docs is a merge gate and the house style explains the why — a cap that counted prose would put those rules in opposition and split files whose code was never the problem. Group by subfolder, not filename prefix. Enforced by tools/lint; classify.rs decides which cap applies; nothing is grandfathered.
nodes.norm_label: size gate — 300 loc source, 150 loc test

nodes.label: Gates vs signals — block on correctness, inform on quality
nodes.rationale: Build, test, clippy -D warnings, golden renders and the size gate prove correctness and are hard gates. Coverage, mutation testing and perf tracking audit quality and are informational signals surfaced where the agent acts on them, never blocking a merge.
nodes.norm_label: gates vs signals — block on correctness, inform on quality

nodes.label: [workspace.lints] — the lint set is chosen, not inherited
nodes.rationale: CI denies warnings, so each lint is a merge gate and must prove correctness or a stated invariant, never a style preference — which is why clippy::pedantic is off: a gate people route around teaches everyone to route around gates. On: unsafe_code=forbid, missing_docs (lib.rs docs are the crate boundaries, so docs are architecture), unreachable_pub, clippy::unwrap_used, dbg_macro, todo. allow-unwrap-in-tests because a failed unwrap in a test is the assertion.
nodes.norm_label: [workspace.lints] — the lint set is chosen, not inherited

nodes.label: One secrets resolver, one order
nodes.rationale: Environment first (exported variable or the gitignored .env documented by .env.example), then the per-machine settings file a shipped build reads. .env is the development path and stops existing once somebody installs a build — that is why there is a second place and why there is still only one resolver. Never in project.json, code or fixtures.

nodes.label: All ffmpeg invocations go through scorsese-render's command builder
nodes.rationale: ffmpeg is an external binary on PATH in dev/CI and bundled beside the binary in shipped builds; that indirection lives in one place, so no ad-hoc Command::new("ffmpeg") anywhere else.
nodes.norm_label: all ffmpeg invocations go through scorsese-render's command builder

nodes.label: Golden-render tests compare frames with tolerance
nodes.rationale: Never byte-equality of encoded output: encoders are not deterministic across versions and platforms, and frames are what we control. Re-blessing a reference to make CI green is never legitimate.
nodes.norm_label: golden-render tests compare frames with tolerance

nodes.label: No real provider calls in tests, ever
nodes.rationale: Veo and ElevenLabs are mocked behind traits and golden-render tests use local fixture media only; a test that spends money or needs a network is a bug.
nodes.norm_label: no real provider calls in tests, ever

nodes.label: Priority by label — architecture → infrastructure → bug → foundation → feature
nodes.rationale: If the way we build isn't solid we halt and fix that first; documentation never waits its turn. Stage labels idea/planning must never be started — the one rule the user's override cannot lift without first removing the label. Increasing derivatives takes precedence over increasing the variables they aim at.
nodes.norm_label: priority by label — architecture → infrastructure → bug → foundation → feature

nodes.label: Timeline framerate — an exact rational, chosen once at `new`
nodes.rationale: 29.97 is 30000/1001, never a rounded float; every clip and keyframe time is a whole frame count on that grid, and the framerate you render at is a separate per-render choice that conforms from the grid.
nodes.norm_label: timeline framerate — an exact rational, chosen once at `new`

nodes.label: Sketch → GO (scorsese generate)
nodes.rationale: Prompt-backed clips start as sketches rendered as slug cards so the whole cut previews for $0; GO generates only sketch and stale assets, reports the cost estimate before spending, and caches by prompt hash so an unchanged prompt is never paid for twice.

nodes.label: [profile.dev] opt-level = 1, dependencies at 3
nodes.rationale: A ten-second 1080p render took 1290 s unoptimised and takes 36 s as configured — it was never a slow compositor, it was an unoptimised one, and measuring the unoptimised build is how 'rendering is slow' turns into folklore. Debug assertions stay on, so a fast render is still a checked one; make release buys the last ~2x (36 s → 19 s), worth it for a delivery, not for iterating on a cut.

nodes.label: The Makefile is the list of gates
nodes.rationale: make help prints format, size, clippy, docs, test, deny and app, each running exactly the command CI runs; every target is runnable alone. make setup points git at .githooks/ so make pre-commit (formatting and size only, under a second) runs before each commit — repository config, so one run covers every worktree, and --no-verify is the deliberate WIP escape.
nodes.norm_label: the makefile is the list of gates

nodes.label: The app gate — the one gate that decides whether to run
nodes.rationale: app/ is its own cargo workspace so a headless change never compiles a graphics dependency tree; make gates runs its format, clippy, build and tests only when the branch touches app/, and says it skipped rather than printing green over a check it chose not to run.
nodes.norm_label: the app gate — the one gate that decides whether to run

nodes.label: make coverage — a signal, not a gate
nodes.rationale: No threshold and it never fails a build. It answers the one question nothing else does — which pub items no test reaches, which clippy's dead_code cannot see because nearly everything in these crates is pub. It does not say whether a test asserts anything; an executed line is not a checked one, and break-testing settles that.
nodes.norm_label: make coverage — a signal, not a gate

nodes.label: The scorsese CLI surface (new, import, assets, probe, check, describe, render, still)
nodes.rationale: Import copies the file into assets/, hashes it and asks ffprobe what it is, so importing the same content twice returns the same asset; probe does the measuring half for assets written straight into project.json by hand or by an agent. Putting clips on tracks still means editing project.json, which is documented and meant to be hand-written.
nodes.norm_label: the scorsese cli surface (new, import, assets, probe, check, describe, render, still)

nodes.label: scorsese check — will this render?
nodes.rationale: Answers about the document and the media it points at: a missing file a clip needs fails; a changed or unprobed file only warns; an unreferenced asset is never worse than a warning because no render can trip over it; sketch clips awaiting generation are the normal pre-GO state and are never reported. --verify adds re-hashing, which costs a read of every file, so it is asked for rather than assumed.

nodes.label: scorsese render — walks the timeline and writes a file
nodes.rationale: Resolution, framerate and bitrate are chosen per render and never stored; sources of another shape are letterboxed rather than stretched and holes render black. --range renders a slice in frames, the cheap way to check one cut. The container and codecs are a render setting the --out extension usually decides, and an unwritable combination is refused before anything is encoded because a plausible-looking wrong file costs more than a refusal.
nodes.norm_label: scorsese render — walks the timeline and writes a file

nodes.label: scorsese describe — reviewing a render without watching it
nodes.rationale: What an unattended agent has instead of eyes: prints the cut stretch by stretch in seconds and frames — what is on screen, on which track, at what fit, what is animated over which half second, what is audible under it, and slug cards with their prompt and state. It costs nothing because the plan works it out anyway, so it runs without ffmpeg before a frame is encoded. What it cannot answer is whether the pixels agree with the project, since it derives from the same document that might be wrong.
nodes.norm_label: scorsese describe — reviewing a render without watching it

nodes.label: scorsese still / --stills — pixels an agent can actually look at
nodes.rationale: --stills decodes PNGs back out of the finished file (the right answer to what the encoder produced, at boundaries where a cut can be one frame wrong) and is an expensive answer to what a frame looks like. `still` composites one instant with the same plan, decoders and compositor and opens no encoder, so the picture cannot disagree with the file; only settings that could change a frame are offered. Over MCP the reply is the image itself, which is what lets an assistant look at an edit instead of reasoning about the JSON.
nodes.norm_label: scorsese still / --stills — pixels an agent can actually look at

nodes.label: Animated clips — opacity, position, scale keyframed per frame
nodes.rationale: Evaluated per frame and drawn by our own compositor rather than ffmpeg. Scale is centre-anchored and a fade is nothing but opacity keyframes, so it composes with a move or a zoom for free. check warns — never fails — when a keyframe track names a property nothing animates, suggesting what the typo probably meant.
nodes.norm_label: animated clips — opacity, position, scale keyframed per frame

nodes.label: Video tracks layer, with fit / fill / native
nodes.rationale: Tracks composite bottom to top in project order, each with its own transforms and opacity, so an overlay is just a clip on a higher track. fit (default) leaves transparency so a narrower clip shows the one beneath; fill crops the overflow; native rests centred at drawn size, which is how a logo is placed. A hole lets lower tracks through; only a stretch empty on every track is black.
nodes.norm_label: video tracks layer, with fit / fill / native

nodes.label: Renders have sound — mixing, volume keyframes, picture decides length
nodes.rationale: Audio tracks are placed, trimmed and summed the way video tracks stack, and volume is an ordinary keyframed property so a fade-out and a mute are one mechanism at different values. A video clip's own audio is mixed too, so muting an interview under a voiceover is volume: 0.0 on that clip. A music bed running past the last shot is cut there and said so in the report, and a project with no audio produces a file with no audio stream — not a stream of silence.
nodes.norm_label: renders have sound — mixing, volume keyframes, picture decides length

nodes.label: Renders draw text — text assets with an inline string and style
nodes.rationale: A text asset carries its string inline plus a style (font, size, colour, alignment, wrap) and the compositor draws it, wrapping what is too wide and ellipsizing what is too tall. It composites like any other layer, so a title fades with opacity and slides with transform.position.* — the same properties a video clip uses.
nodes.norm_label: renders draw text — text assets with an inline string and style

nodes.label: Shipped fonts — Liberation Sans / Serif under crates/compositor/fonts
nodes.rationale: Shipped rather than resolved from the system because a system font resolves to a different file on every platform, and text has to render identically everywhere for the golden-render gate to mean anything. They are defaults, not the vocabulary — font may name a file the project carries. Outlines are read with skrifa and filled by the same tiny-skia rasteriser every other layer goes through.
nodes.norm_label: shipped fonts — liberation sans / serif under crates/compositor/fonts

nodes.label: The 200-800 axis range splits document validation from what only the file can answer
nodes.norm_label: the 200-800 axis range splits document validation from what only the file can answer

nodes.label: Nothing depends on crates/golden, so the fixture font is duplicated deliberately
nodes.norm_label: nothing depends on crates/golden, so the fixture font is duplicated deliberately

nodes.label: Golden renders (pixel gate)
nodes.rationale: Pixels regress silently and no human eye is in the loop for an agent-driven PR, so a hard green-to-merge gate inside cargo test --workspace is what stands between 'CI is green' and 'the video is right'.

nodes.label: Golden fixture
nodes.rationale: A directory under crates/golden/fixtures/ holding a real project.json (the format is part of what is tested), a fixture.json recipe, and reference frames; description exists so a future reader can judge whether re-blessing was legitimate.

nodes.label: fixture.json (media recipe and frame selection)
nodes.rationale: Names how to conjure the media, how to render, and which frames to compare; boundaries (last frame of a clip, first of the next) are chosen because that is where an off-by-one hides — sampling the middle of a long clip asserts almost nothing.

nodes.label: expected/ reference PNG frames
nodes.rationale: References are PNGs so a change arrives in review as an image diff — the only form in which a human can judge whether it was legitimate.

nodes.label: expected/decoder.txt provenance record
nodes.rationale: Never fails and never warns on a passing run: failing would make the suite unrunnable for anyone on a different distro's ffmpeg, and warning on every green run trains everyone to scroll past. It speaks only inside a failing fixture's report, as context and not permission to re-bless.

nodes.label: Media generated at test time from lavfi
nodes.rationale: Synthetic ffmpeg sources keep sample footage out of the repository; flat colours also give swscale nothing to disagree about across decoder versions. The only committed exception is a font, which no lavfi source can ever produce.
nodes.norm_label: media generated at test time from lavfi

nodes.label: SSIM on the worst 8x8 luma block
nodes.rationale: Catches where pixels are — a shape half a pixel out, a soft edge, a wrong patch in one corner.
nodes.norm_label: ssim on the worst 8x8 luma block

nodes.label: Mean absolute error per colour channel
nodes.rationale: Catches what pixels are — a wrong colour, a frame a few levels bright, a cut one frame early.
nodes.norm_label: mean absolute error per colour channel

nodes.label: Comparison tolerances (min_ssim 0.95, max_mean_error 2.0)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately loose enough to survive another platform's x264 and far tighter than any real regression (red against blue scores 0.70 / 169). Sized for encoder noise only, which is why decoder differences are handled separately.

nodes.label: scorsese_render::frames
nodes.rationale: Frame extraction is a shipped capability rather than harness-owned code; nothing may depend on crates/golden, so the harness is a caller. Every fixture passing unchanged across that move is what proved the two were the same code.

nodes.label: scorsese render --stills
nodes.rationale: Asks what came back out of the delivered file — it writes PNGs through the same frames code the golden harness uses.

nodes.label: scorsese still (not a shortcut for the gate)
nodes.rationale: It composites a frame without opening an encoder, which is what makes it fast and useless here: the gate exists to catch what a delivered file holds. Swapping it in would quietly narrow what the fixtures prove.
nodes.norm_label: scorsese still (not a shortcut for the gate)

nodes.label: Re-blessing (UPDATE_GOLDENS=1)
nodes.rationale: Legitimate only when the render changed on purpose and the new frames are what was intended; never as a way to make CI green. A golden gate re-blessed reflexively is worse than no gate because it still reads as coverage.

nodes.label: A missing reference fails rather than being created
nodes.rationale: A fixture with nothing to compare against would otherwise pass by asserting nothing — an untested fixture sitting in the repo looking like coverage is the failure mode the whole document exists to prevent.
nodes.norm_label: a missing reference fails rather than being created

nodes.label: CI pins ubuntu-24.04 runner image
nodes.rationale: A moving label would swap the decoder under the pixel gate by a major version the day GitHub rolls it, with nothing in any diff to say so — the same reasoning as rust-toolchain.toml. Every run also prints ffmpeg -version.

nodes.label: Audio property tests (crates/render/tests/audio)
nodes.rationale: No committed reference waveform: resampled lossy audio is not reproducible sample for sample, and a binary reference nobody can read is one nobody can check. 'Is there sound here, and is it getting louder' has an obvious right answer.

nodes.label: crates/golden/tests/comparing.rs
nodes.rationale: Pins to specific cases that neither SSIM nor mean error alone is enough and each catches what the other waves through.

nodes.label: crates/golden/tests/provenance.rs
nodes.rationale: Holds both halves of the decoder-record rule, including that a fixture whose record names a different ffmpeg still passes when its frames match.

nodes.label: scorsese-mcp server
nodes.rationale: Exposes scorsese so an assistant can read, change and render a project without a person typing commands; a plain binary over stdin/stdout, nothing to configure and no port to pick.

nodes.label: Model Context Protocol
nodes.rationale: A protocol, not a Claude feature: Claude is what the server is developed and tested against, not a dependency, the way an HTTP API does not care whether a browser or curl is calling.

nodes.label: Point the client at the crate, not the built artifact
nodes.rationale: cargo run costs a fraction of a second when current and picks up a git pull with nothing to remember; the tradeoff genuinely reverses for a shipped binary, which should not need a toolchain or a compile to start.
nodes.norm_label: point the client at the crate, not the built artifact

nodes.label: The tool list is fixed at handshake and never re-announced
nodes.rationale: 'Am I running the current server?' is unanswerable from inside the protocol, so a stale binary's missing capability is not merely absent but unfindable — the run routes around it, finishes, and reports success while being slower and dumber than the repo it ran from.
nodes.norm_label: the tool list is fixed at handshake and never re-announced

nodes.label: Generated tools table
nodes.rationale: Rows are read out of the registry by `make mcp-table` so a row is never a claim the server would not make itself; everything under the table is hand-written because it is about how tools relate, which no single tool knows.

nodes.label: project_new tool
nodes.rationale: Refuses a non-empty directory and writes nothing at all when it refuses: half a project laid over what was there is worse than an error, with no way afterwards to tell which half is whose.

nodes.label: project_read tool
nodes.rationale: The edit is the document: the whole cut is one JSON file, so any change is read it, change it, write it back.

nodes.label: project_write tool
nodes.rationale: Validates before writing and lists every problem, leaving the file exactly as it was, so a half-formed edit cannot destroy a working one.

nodes.label: project_probe tool
nodes.rationale: An asset written straight into project.json carries a path and nothing measured, so features needing the source's own length must skip it; probing is safe after every edit because an already-probed asset is left alone.

nodes.label: import tool
nodes.rationale: Copies media in and records the relative path it landed at — the caller's path is never written down, which is why a project survives scp -r. A directory imports its contents, non-recursively, sorted by name, skipping and naming non-media; every rejection is found before the first byte is copied.

nodes.label: The script (script_read / script_write)
nodes.rationale: A file beside project.json rather than a field inside it, so it needs its own tools, unlike a note which lives on the element it is about. Read it before touching the edit: it holds the reasons no timeline can show. `scorsese new` leaves no stub so no project falsely claims to carry one.

nodes.label: dissolve tool
nodes.rationale: Sugar that writes ordinary keyframes which stay visible and editable, adding no renderer stage, so a dissolve composes with a move for free. It moves the incoming clip to a track above because two clips on one track may not overlap, and says so in the reply.

nodes.label: scale_pacing tool
nodes.rationale: Durations scale only where that is free; for a clip with a real file behind it the instruction is ambiguous (show less vs play faster) and picking silently is the failure that looks successful either way, so those clips keep their length and are named in the reply.

nodes.label: still tool (what the edit looks like)
nodes.rationale: The render pipeline with the encoder taken out. `at` takes a list because a picture is the most expensive reply the server sends and one round trip per section decides how often anything gets verified; `out` with a list is refused because a path names one file.
nodes.norm_label: still tool (what the edit looks like)

nodes.label: look tool (what is in the footage)
nodes.rationale: One contact sheet, not five images: what tells you what a shot does is the change between frames, visible only side by side. Takes a path rather than an asset id so footage is looked at before the decision to import it.
nodes.norm_label: look tool (what is in the footage)

nodes.label: generate tool
nodes.rationale: The one tool that costs money, so: dry_run quotes without a key, video and narration are quoted on separate lines and never averaged, a key is asked for only by the half that has work, one failed brief leaves the rest generated, and collect can never spend anything.

nodes.label: voices tool
nodes.rationale: There is no default voice and never will be: every ElevenLabs default voice expires 2026-12-31, so a hardcoded id is a guaranteed outage with a date on it. A listing always states its age, and nothing is ever silently substituted for a dead id.

nodes.label: voice_design tool
nodes.rationale: One call, three candidates, one charge on the preview text; spend is its own line item so a generation total never moves while nobody is generating. The voice lives in the user's account, so description and seed are recorded in designed-voices.json — the id travels with scp -r and the voice does not. Voice cloning is excluded by decision, not omission.

nodes.label: synth_set tool
nodes.rationale: Tuning is a float at a time and synth_write prices that at the entire piece; it addresses only named things (bpm, seed, swing, gain by track name) because notes and entries have no names and positions shift the moment one is inserted.

nodes.label: synth_bake tool
nodes.rationale: Nothing marks an asset stale: a bake is named for the hash of its recipe, so changing the recipe changes which file the asset wants. Reports a row per track post-gain, always in the reply, because a report that must be asked for is one an unattended client never sees.

nodes.label: audio_level tool
nodes.rationale: Closes the one loop that terminates at a human. Comparison against a previous file is the part with teeth because an absolute number is hard to judge and a difference is not. A signal and never a gate: there is no correct loudness, and a metric treated as an ear produces music that optimises the number.

nodes.label: synth_survey tool
nodes.rationale: The only tool reading more than one recipe: six cues can each pass every per-bake check and still be one instrument. Ranks loudest by gain x duty rather than written gain, or percussion crowns the list; it counts and stops, with no diversity score, because that is exactly the metric that would get optimised.

nodes.label: render tool (with range)
nodes.rationale: Checking one ten-second cue in a sixty-second cut should cost ten seconds of encoding; the range parser is the CLI's own, so a range either client refuses is refused by both with the same words.

nodes.label: Stateless, on purpose
nodes.rationale: No server-side 'open project': every call names its project, so a client may crash, reconnect, or run two conversations against one project without anything getting out of step.

nodes.label: crates/mcp/tests/described.rs
nodes.rationale: A description is the entire interface a client has; an undescribed tool is a capability that cannot be found — nothing fails, the assistant simply never calls it. So the registry is walked and a useless description fails the build.

nodes.label: crates/mcp/tests/table.rs
nodes.rationale: A tool missing from the page was the same failure by another door and no test caught it, so the page is held to the registry — which gives a description's first sentence a second job as the table cell.

nodes.label: Generations keyed by hash of the brief
nodes.rationale: The hash covers every field including the bytes of every still named, so a repeat call after a dropped connection costs nothing, while swapping face.png for a different picture of the same name is correctly a new brief.
nodes.norm_label: generations keyed by hash of the brief

nodes.label: Mutation testing
nodes.rationale: Coverage answers 'was this line executed'; mutation answers 'if this line were wrong, would anything notice'. A line can be executed by ten tests and asserted on by none — as when Gain::at's body became a constant and the volume-ramp test stayed green.

nodes.label: cargo-mutants
nodes.rationale: Edits one small thing, rebuilds, runs the tests. Use -F (--re) not -f: --file is unioned with examine_globs and widens the run instead of narrowing it. Survivors land in mutants.out/missed.txt with the surviving edit in mutants.out/diff/.

nodes.label: A signal, never a gate
nodes.rationale: The mutants CI job is continue-on-error and nothing it finds can block a merge. Deliberate, not a soft start: a gate that regularly demands a fix for something already fine teaches everyone to route around it, and then it means nothing.

nodes.label: Equivalent mutants
nodes.rationale: Changes that alter the code without altering behaviour, which no test can catch — a value clamped straight back into range, a default another branch always overwrites, a derive-adjacent helper with one caller.

nodes.label: Break-testing
nodes.rationale: The complement: mutation asks whether anything asserts this at all, break-testing asks whether the assertion pins the right behaviour. Two of three real gaps here were semantic (a bed restarting instead of resuming, keyframes timed from the timeline) and no generated mutant would have surfaced them.

nodes.label: .cargo/mutants.toml
nodes.rationale: The authority on what is mutated, with a written reason for every inclusion and exclusion, and where an equivalent mutant is recorded as an exclude_re entry. Read it rather than the doc's summary — the config is the thing that runs.

nodes.label: Mutated surface (pure logic only)
nodes.rationale: crates/core, crates/compositor and the plan and audio arithmetic of crates/render; ffmpeg command builders and crates/golden are excluded on purpose. Per PR the run is narrowed again with --in-diff so cost tracks the change, not the codebase.

nodes.label: Triaging a survivor
nodes.rationale: A survivor is a test gap until shown equivalent: read the diff, name an input where the mutant differs, write that assertion in the file already covering the function. Weakening or deleting an assertion to quiet the report is never correct, and fixing survivors in code the PR did not write belongs in its own issue.

nodes.label: OutputFormat
nodes.rationale: Container and codecs became an explicit setting because they used to be made by accident: `--out cut.wmv` produced ASF carrying H.264 and said nothing after spending the whole encode. For an unattended agent a plausible-looking wrong file is far more expensive than a refusal.

nodes.label: RenderSettings
nodes.rationale: The delivered shape sits beside resolution, fps and bitrate: chosen per render and never stored, because project.json describes the edit, not the deliverable.

nodes.label: Container / codec table (mp4, mkv, avi, wmv)
nodes.rationale: The first codec in each row is the container's default. avi's optional h264 row is the whole point of the setting — container and codec are separate decisions; wmv refuses anything but wmv2/wmav2 because anything else in a .wmv is not a Windows Media file a viewer would accept.
nodes.norm_label: container / codec table (mp4, mkv, avi, wmv)

nodes.label: Extension is a default, --container wins
nodes.rationale: Naming the file is usually the whole decision, so every invocation written before the setting existed still means what it meant; the muxer is pinned with ffmpeg's -f so the file is what the setting says whatever it is called.

nodes.label: Refusal where the setting is built
nodes.rationale: Structural rather than a check somebody must remember: an OutputFormat cannot be constructed around a combination we do not write, so it has no way to reach an encoder — refused before the project is opened and minutes before anything would have been encoded.
nodes.norm_label: refusal where the setting is built

nodes.label: crates/render/tests/formats/
nodes.rationale: Holds the page to the code in both directions: a documented row the code does not write, or a codec the code writes that the page never mentions, fails the build.

nodes.label: Only encoders already required or built into ffmpeg
nodes.rationale: 'Whatever ffmpeg has' is not defensible: which ffmpeg is a shipping decision (distro build in dev and CI, bundled Tauri sidecar when shipped) and a licensing one. A short list we test beats a long list we assume; avi and wmv exist to prove the mechanism generalises, and webm is the likelier next ask.
nodes.norm_label: only encoders already required or built into ffmpeg

nodes.label: Every cost figure is an estimate, never a bill
nodes.rationale: No provider reports what a generation cost, so every total scorsese prints is arithmetic over a copied rate table. Naming the field what-it-cost when it means what-we-worked-out-it-would-cost is quiet wrongness only noticed by the person who already paid.
nodes.norm_label: every cost figure is an estimate, never a bill

nodes.label: Rate — a price with the day it was checked
nodes.rationale: Both fields are required so a price cannot be added without saying when somebody read it; a price with no date is a price nobody can audit. Rate::cents_per_second is whole cents because every rate Veo publishes happens to be a whole number of cents per second.
nodes.norm_label: rate — a price with the day it was checked

nodes.label: Staleness at 180 days — a signal, never a gate
nodes.rationale: Blocks nothing, per CLAUDE.md's gates-versus-signals rule, and because a figure being old does not make it wrong. 180 days is a judgement, not a rule: vendors reprice on no schedule.
nodes.norm_label: staleness at 180 days — a signal, never a gate

nodes.label: Veo 3.1 shot rates (US$ per second)
nodes.rationale: A list of rows rather than a grid, because Lite has no 4k and a grid cell would have to hold a price for something that cannot be bought; asking answers `Unpriced`. Rows scorsese does not offer (Standard, 4k) stay in so the vendor's price list can be ticked through.

nodes.label: ElevenLabs narration rates (cents per 1000 characters)
nodes.rationale: Priced before the call, not after it: a line is priced by text already in the document. Turbo is omitted because the vendor's own docs recommend Flash over Turbo in every case — offering both would be offering a choice with a right answer. Voice Library credit multipliers are ignored deliberately: modelling a credit system to move an advisory counter by cents is not worth keeping true.

nodes.label: `estimated_cost_cents` asset field
nodes.rationale: Renamed from `cost_cents` after two days: these are summed into a project total shown to somebody deciding whether to spend more.

nodes.label: Whole US cents all the way through
nodes.rationale: A total is a sum, and a sum of floats is not the same number twice; a ceiling off by a rounding error is a ceiling nobody can reason about. Covers the rate table, estimated_cost_cents and budget_cents.
nodes.norm_label: whole us cents all the way through

nodes.label: Narration estimates round up
nodes.rationale: Rounding down would let a run slip past the ceiling a fraction of a cent at a time, and a ceiling that can be crossed a little at a time is not a ceiling. Costs at most a cent per line.

nodes.label: No provider reports what a generation cost
nodes.rationale: A finished Veo operation carries a URI and nothing else — no amount, no usage record. Actual spend exists only in Google Cloud Billing, a day late, aggregated per SKU, unattributable to the shot that caused it; no endpoint closes that gap.
nodes.norm_label: no provider reports what a generation cost

nodes.label: `project.json` — schema v16
nodes.rationale: The contract between CLI, MCP server, GUI and every saved project; meant to be hand-written so an agent can author a whole video without a mouse. Unknown fields are an error rather than a warning so a typo like `trackz` fails the load. Changing the format is architecture work needing a schema_version bump and a migration note; this build reads exactly one schema version and refuses the rest.

nodes.label: `timeline_fps` — rational timeline grid
nodes.rationale: Rational, not float: 29.97 is exactly 30000/1001 and rounding it is where long-timeline drift comes from. Required with no default because a missing framerate leaves every time in the file meaning something other than intended. Chosen at project creation; changing it later is a real operation, not a field edit.

nodes.label: Conforming — source fps ≠ timeline fps
nodes.rationale: Nearest source frame in wall-clock time, no interpolation: 24→30 repeats frames in the 2:3 pattern. Optical-flow retiming is a feature someone can ask for, not a silent default.

nodes.label: `script` — the document the edit is cut from
nodes.rationale: A path rather than an inline string because such a document is long (30 KB against a 34 KB project.json) and a file gets a readable diff. Never parsed: the moment something extracted meaning it would become a format with rules and stop being the place you write freely. A missing file is a warning — a project that has lost its brief should still render.
nodes.norm_label: `script` — the document the edit is cut from

nodes.label: `note` — why, on anything with an `id`
nodes.rationale: Neither script nor note ever renders — an invariant, tested by rendering with and without and failing on a single differing byte. Attaches to an element, never to a span of time, because a timed note desynchronises silently the first time the cut is retimed. A note dies with its element, and that is the feature: nothing to garbage collect.

nodes.label: Asset — an entity clips point at by id
nodes.rationale: Clips reference assets by id and never by path, so re-importing or regenerating a file is one edit in one place. An asset carries exactly the brief its kind takes and never the other — a `recipe` on a Veo asset is refused rather than ignored.
nodes.norm_label: asset — an entity clips point at by id

nodes.label: `generated_audio` asset (ElevenLabs voice)
nodes.rationale: Until generated it contributes silence to the mix, but its slug card still shows for exactly the frames its clip covers, so a cut built around a voice-over can be watched before a word is paid for.

nodes.label: `synth_audio` asset — sound from a recipe
nodes.rationale: Free, keyless, networkless and deterministic, so the generated file is named for the SHA-256 of the recipe's bytes and a path pointing at a hash the recipe no longer has *is* what stale means for this kind. Does not replace generated_audio: no amount of arithmetic will read a line aloud.

nodes.label: `text` asset — content inline, no file
nodes.rationale: Text meant to be seen is a text asset — that is what keeps script and note off the screen. Has no animatable properties of its own: a title that slides and fades uses transform.position and opacity, the same as any clip. `fit` is meaningless on it since there is no source raster to reconcile.

nodes.label: `color` asset — appearance without content
nodes.rationale: Replaces generating a PNG of identical pixels; fills whatever raster the render is, so it is resolution-independent by construction. No default colour — a background that came out white because nobody chose would be a shot rendered wrong that no error mentioned. Gradients are a different feature wearing this one's clothes.

nodes.label: `style` — how a text asset looks
nodes.rationale: Measurements are fractions of the raster, not pixels, because resolution is a render setting: 72px would be a different title at every size. `sans` and `serif` are reserved (Liberation Sans/Serif, committed to the repo) because a system font lookup resolves differently on every platform.

nodes.label: `style.weight` — the variable-font axis
nodes.rationale: Most modern open fonts ship only as variable files whose default instance is often not Regular (Manrope 200, Outfit 100), so a variable font with no weight is refused by name rather than falling back — the rule being held is that a project which renders wrong must not render silently. No clamping (that is silent substitution one step along); only the wght axis is read, since optical size, width and slant are not what 'make this bold' means.

nodes.label: `media` — what something measured, never what anyone chose
nodes.rationale: Filled by `scorsese probe`/`project_probe`/import, never hand-written. A still deliberately carries size but no duration_seconds or frame_rate, because ffprobe invents both for a one-frame video and how long a still is on screen is the clip's business. An unprobed asset bounds no clip — a ceiling applying to half the pool would be worse than none.
nodes.norm_label: `media` — what something measured, never what anyone chose

nodes.label: Slug card — a generated brief standing in for media
nodes.rationale: What makes previewing a full cut cost nothing. Drawn for sketch, queued, stale, and for a generated asset whose file has gone — a preview with one card is worth more than no preview. A slug card is a stand-in, never a caption.
nodes.norm_label: slug card — a generated brief standing in for media

nodes.label: `video` — the rest of a shot's brief
nodes.rationale: Stills are named by asset id, never by path, so a project survives being copied and the brief hash can cover a still's sha256. Conflicting combinations are refused by `scorsese check` before submission — a request that could never succeed should cost a message, not a round trip — and reference_images on `lite` is refused rather than honoured with images dropped, because it is the one change that invalidates a brief rather than cheapening it.
nodes.norm_label: `video` — the rest of a shot's brief

nodes.label: `speech` — how a line is said
nodes.rationale: Models are named for what the choice is about (expressive/standard/fast) rather than vendor version strings. `language` on the standard model is refused even though the vendor accepts it — the API takes it, charges, drops the field, and the failure has no symptom except somebody listening. A separate block from `video` because the two share no field, and one `generation` block would have a legal shape depending on `kind`. Characters counted as characters, not bytes, for Portuguese.

nodes.label: `voice_id` — the field with no possible default
nodes.rationale: Every vendor Default voice expires 2026-12-31 and the set is being replaced, so a fallback in the format would be a guaranteed outage with a date on it. A narration with no voice is a legitimate document, refused at the moment of spending rather than of writing.
nodes.norm_label: `voice_id` — the field with no possible default

nodes.label: Brief hash — what makes an asset stale
nodes.rationale: Every field of `video`/`speech` is hashed with the prompt, so editing one makes the asset stale exactly as rewording does. Timestamps are excluded on purpose: a timestamp inside a hash would make an unchanged prompt look edited and bill for it again, and one read by the compositor would make a golden render depend on the day it ran.
nodes.norm_label: brief hash — what makes an asset stale

nodes.label: Track — video composites, audio sums
nodes.rationale: Order means nothing on audio tracks because addition does not care which came first. A video clip's own sound is mixed at the same keyframed volume, so muting a talking head is volume 0.0 — no new field, no demuxing by hand. A hole contributes nothing so lower tracks show through; only a stretch empty on every video track renders black. Picture decides a render's length.

nodes.label: Clip — whole frames on the timeline grid
nodes.rationale: Times are whole frames, not seconds: a clip ending at 240 and one starting at 240 do not overlap, and nothing has to arbitrate a cut at 1.0333333. A fractional or negative time fails the parse rather than being rounded. A clip may not show source that is not there, bounded by the media block the document already carries.
nodes.norm_label: clip — whole frames on the timeline grid

nodes.label: `fit` — how a source meets the raster
nodes.rationale: Leftover is transparent rather than black so an upper 4:3 clip over a 16:9 one shows the wider clip at the sides. `native` exists because under `fit` a 64×64 logo arrives 1080×1080 and needs transform.scale 0.06 — a number that means nothing, stops being right when the render resolution changes, and requires arithmetic against a raster the project is not supposed to know about.
nodes.norm_label: `fit` — how a source meets the raster

nodes.label: `crop` — a rectangle of the source, in fractions
nodes.rationale: The asset is never touched — cutting the file down loses the original pixels, records nothing about what was removed, and makes sha256 and media describe a file no capture ever produced. Fractions rather than source pixels so a crop survives the asset being replaced by a higher-resolution capture, and is checkable from the document alone. Crop happens before fit; cropping after would be cropping the output, which is a matte.
nodes.norm_label: `crop` — a rectangle of the source, in fractions

nodes.label: `anchor` — which edge a position is measured from
nodes.rationale: Without it the format can say where a layer ended up and not what was meant: a title column beside a picture becomes an offset derived on paper that nobody can read back, and lengthening the title moves it. A positive offset always moves the layer further in, so flipping a layout is one word. A field rather than an animatable property, because animating how a coordinate is read would slide a layer by changing what its number means.
nodes.norm_label: `anchor` — which edge a position is measured from

nodes.label: `speed` — source frames against timeline frames
nodes.rationale: Breaks the one-to-one relation source_in and duration used to have, deliberately: halving a clip's length to cover the same footage is an operation a GUI performs, and the document stays declarative so a clip can be sped up and trimmed without the two fighting. Speed changes pitch, as an editor expects; keyframes stay in timeline time so a fade written half a second in stays there at any speed.

nodes.label: Keyframes — (property_path, [(t, value, easing)])
nodes.rationale: `t` counts from the clip's start so moving a clip never rewrites its keyframes. Core does not check that a property path exists — core defines property types, never property values — but an unanimated path is warned about, because ignoring `opactiy` silently means the render succeeds and the fade never happens. Never an error: a project authored against a newer scorsese must still render on an older one. Frames are enough resolution because keyframes are control points; volume is evaluated per sample so a ramp is not a zipper.

nodes.label: `by` — the tool that signed a keyframe track
nodes.rationale: Buys exactly one thing: a generator may replace tracks it signed and must never touch unsigned or foreign ones. Without it a generator can only clobber everything or refuse to run twice, and both make the edit-and-listen loop unusable. Absent means hand-written; present but blank is an error.
nodes.norm_label: `by` — the tool that signed a keyframe track

nodes.label: `scorsese duck` — auto-ducking under narration
nodes.rationale: Triggers on the narration clip's extents rather than on the sound, so a cut can be ducked, watched and judged before a word of voice-over has been paid for. Two close lines become a single dip because coming up and immediately back down is pumping.

nodes.label: Project-relative paths and the four directories
nodes.rationale: Absolute paths, backslashes and `..` are rejected so a project survives `scp -r` between machines. The rule covers every path in the document — a style's font, a synth_audio's recipe, the script — not just `path`. generated/ and cache/ can be remade; recipes/ cannot, and assets/ originals live elsewhere.
nodes.norm_label: project-relative paths and the four directories

nodes.label: Validation — the document, and only the document
nodes.rationale: load validates and save does not, so an editor may save work mid-edit. Every problem is reported in one pass so an agent repairing unattended sees the whole list. Validation never opens a file: whether media exists is `scorsese check`'s question, which is why an unprobed asset bounds nothing and the answer to a missing ceiling is `scorsese probe` rather than a slower load.
nodes.norm_label: validation — the document, and only the document

nodes.label: Atomic save — write beside, rename into place
nodes.rationale: More than one program is looking — MCP's project_read is stateless, the GUI writes when a hand comes off a clip — and there is no journal to recover from: this one file is the edit. Recipes and baked media go the same way.
nodes.norm_label: atomic save — write beside, rename into place

nodes.label: CI doc gate — marked json blocks and published properties
nodes.rationale: The compositor and mixer publish what they animate and a test asserts the table matches both ways, so documenting a property that does not exist fails the build. Unmarked json blocks fail rather than quietly escaping the check. What none of it proves is that the prose is true — written down so a green check is never mistaken for an accurate page.
nodes.norm_label: ci doc gate — marked json blocks and published properties

nodes.label: Prompts — provider behaviour learned by paying
nodes.rationale: A recipe is cheap to be wrong about; a prompt is paid for before anyone finds out. Not a cookbook or style guide — only provider behaviour that cannot be guessed from outside, each entry with the incident behind it, because the incident is what lets the next reader tell whether their case is the same one. Mirror image of #189 on the free side (recipes.md says how a source is built, never what it sounds like).
nodes.norm_label: prompts — provider behaviour learned by paying

nodes.label: Never name the medium
nodes.rationale: 'shot on grainy 16mm film' made Veo render the film object — sprocket holes and edge codes inside the picture on all three Summit Scene 1 shots, recovered with a per-clip crop that permanently trims a frame bought at full size. Describe the image instead: era, grain, lens.

nodes.label: Slow motion is bought, not applied
nodes.rationale: `speed` redistributes frames that already exist; Veo asked for slow motion renders motion samples a normal-speed generation would never contain — 60fps at 0.5× versus 120fps played at 60. For generated footage speed is the fallback, not the plan.
nodes.norm_label: slow motion is bought, not applied

nodes.label: Keep colour neutral if the shot will be graded
nodes.rationale: Asking Veo for the grade bakes it into a file that cannot be regenerated without paying again, so 'a little less brown' stops being an edit and becomes a purchase. Grading today is an ffmpeg pass outside the project, filed as #250.
nodes.norm_label: keep colour neutral if the shot will be graded

nodes.label: Veo 3.1 generates sound whether the prompt mentions it or not
nodes.rationale: Audio arrives regardless and is paid for either way, chosen by something that has not read the rest of the cut — so naming the sound is taking back a decision, not asking for an extra.
nodes.norm_label: veo 3.1 generates sound whether the prompt mentions it or not

nodes.label: Veo outputs 24 fps
nodes.rationale: A project at the default 30 conforms every generated shot with 2:3 repetition, so the judder lands on exactly the footage that cost money. `scorsese new film.scor --fps 24` for a cut built mostly of generated shots — the rate is not a field edit afterwards.

nodes.label: Recipe — sound from a document
nodes.rationale: JSON under recipes/, free, keyless, networkless and byte-deterministic, so a project can carry its whole sound design as text and rebuild it anywhere. Only what would produce silence, a divide-by-zero, an unstable filter or an unbounded allocation is refused; musical taste is not checked and an ugly patch renders.

nodes.label: `patch` recipe — one instrument, one note
nodes.rationale: `note` lives in the document because which pitch is part of what the asset is — a footstep and a gunshot can be one instrument at different pitches. `seed` re-rolls stochastic sources: same seed, same bytes, forever.

nodes.label: `song` recipe — beats, patterns, arrangement
nodes.rationale: Everything is beats, never seconds, so changing tempo is one number. Write repetition as repetition: the same music as one flat note list is hundreds of lines and every edit becomes a merge conflict with itself. A track's patch may be inline or a project-relative path so songs can share an instrument.

nodes.label: The fixed signal path: source → filter → amp → fx
nodes.rationale: Fixed and in this order: a recipe chooses what fills each stage, never how they connect. Four source kinds (osc_stack, karplus, noise, fm2), one LFO target, and a limiter that always runs after the fx and is not listed — a bake must not clip, and that is not the recipe's decision.
nodes.norm_label: the fixed signal path: source → filter → amp → fx

nodes.label: Playing harder, not just louder — `vel_cutoff` and `vel_index`
nodes.rationale: Velocity as a pure fader is a large part of why a carefully written synth part still sounds like a machine: a real instrument gets brighter, not merely louder, and the ear reads that as effort. They add rather than scale, so each source of movement stays independent and a zero stays harmless; negative is legal and means velocity darkens.
nodes.norm_label: playing harder, not just louder — `vel_cutoff` and `vel_index`

nodes.label: Arrangement transforms — `transpose`, `vel_scale`, `tracks`
nodes.rationale: Without them the format prices variation out — a repeat costs one word and a variation a whole pattern — so songs come out four thin patterns played twice each, for the same reason water runs downhill. Transforms do not stack (every entry transforms the pattern as written) so the tenth repeat is not nine octaves up; `tracks` is a filter, not a remap, or a pattern would mean something different depending on where it was played.

nodes.label: `swing` and `humanize` — playing it, not clocking it
nodes.rationale: Exact beats at exact velocities is the loudest thing a generated piece says about itself. Swing stretches the beat around the off-beat so finer subdivisions ride along and no two notes swap places; humanize's timing is in seconds because a player is not three times sloppier at 40 bpm. Both draw from the same per-note seed chain in arrangement order, so the piece stays byte-identical yet a repeat is not a photocopy.
nodes.norm_label: `swing` and `humanize` — playing it, not clocking it

nodes.label: Where an effect goes — patch, track, or song
nodes.rationale: Most of the difference between some synth parts and a piece of music. Reverb belongs on the song: on a patch each instrument is in its own room, drifting apart the moment one is tuned, and it is one room convolved once instead of per note. A song chain runs before the limiter always — nothing may add gain after the thing guaranteeing a bake does not clip.
nodes.norm_label: where an effect goes — patch, track, or song

nodes.label: Bake — `generated/<sha256 of the recipe's bytes>.wav`
nodes.rationale: That naming is the whole cache: the path an asset holds is the record of which recipe produced it, so editing a recipe makes the asset stale by arithmetic and nobody has to mark it. Output is mono 16-bit 44.1 kHz and mono is settled, not a stage toward stereo — a recipe places a sound in time, never in space. `fit`/`fade`/`tail` fit a song to the cut; stretch refuses beyond 25% because a bed at 40% speed is not a bed.

nodes.label: `synth survey` — what the whole set is made of
nodes.rationale: Every column is written, not measured, so it costs no bake — the cheapest signal in the project and the one with least excuse for being missing. The second half of a track row (duty, sustain, notes per second, median pitch) exists because the source kind does not predict what anyone hears: three different kinds can be one plucked guitar to a listener. It counts and stops — no diversity number, because a metric treated as an ear gets optimised.
nodes.norm_label: `synth survey` — what the whole set is made of

nodes.label: 'Loudest' means gain × duty
nodes.rationale: Written gain alone is a per-note peak and percussion is written loud exactly because it is short. Ranked by gain alone the rollup once crowned a hi-hat in two songs of six and reported a more varied set than the one on disk — the exact wrong answer, since a client with no ears takes the line literally and stops looking. Still a proxy, not an ear: transients carry prominence no written number knows about.

nodes.label: Loudness measurement is a signal and never a gate
nodes.rationale: There is no correct loudness — a sting is meant to be hot, a bed far down — so a threshold refusing a bake would be a taste enforced as a build failure. Measurement finds defects, not taste, and a metric treated as an ear produces music that optimises the number. Per-track rows turn '87% below 250 Hz' from an unactionable diagnosis into an address; `--against` is the form with the most teeth, because an absolute number is hard to judge and a difference is not.
nodes.norm_label: loudness measurement is a signal and never a gate

nodes.label: Recipes make no voice — the free/paid boundary
nodes.rationale: Nothing in a patch or a song has anywhere to put a phoneme, and a synthesised approximation of a person talking is not what anyone wants when real narration is one asset away. Keeping the two kinds apart is what lets everything on the recipes page promise free and deterministic.
nodes.norm_label: recipes make no voice — the free/paid boundary
